plain: Colorado already charges state sales tax on sporting goods such as bikes, camping gear, boats and fishing equipment. Proposition 137 would send part of that money, about $175 million a year, to conservation, wildfire and outdoor programs.

short_version.text: Proposition 137 raises no tax and no price. It sets aside about $175 million a year of sales tax already collected on sporting goods for wildfire, watershed, parks and outdoor programs. The cost falls on TABOR refunds in years when there are refunds, and on other state programs in years when there aren't.

agree_means: Agreeing means voting yes on Proposition 137. Prices and tax rates stay the same, about $175 million a year goes to land, wildfire and outdoor programs, and TABOR refunds shrink in years when refunds are paid.
disagree_means: Disagreeing means voting no. The sales tax money stays in the general budget, where lawmakers spend it each year or the state refunds it under TABOR.

research_notes: No source in this file needed the browser. For a reviewer: (1) The Blue Book says Proposition 137 would end a six-tier sales-tax refund worth $26-$83 (single) and $52-$166 (joint) in at least 2027-28. NN's Table 1 lists different current-law refunds ($21-$65 single for 2027). They are different mechanisms and tax years, so check with Legislative Council before putting them side by side. The Common Sense Institute says tax year 2029; the Blue Book says 2027; I used the Blue Book. (2) 'Roughly $21 million now' is my sum of $16.4 million (wildfire) and $5 million (watershed) from the Blue Book. (3) The $6-per-$1 mitigation figure is a campaign spokesperson's citation of a 2018 report that I did not fetch. (4) Campaign money is from Oct. 6 filings as reported by Post Independent. (5) I found no independent estimate of jobs or GDP effects, so there is no economy item. (6) The web search budget ran out before I could look for more on the opposition.
